blocks.text: This module introduces the everyday habits and decisions that help protect people, information and technology at work. It explains cybersecurity in practical language so employees can recognise common risks, choose safer actions and report concerns early. The focus is on responsible behaviour rather than technical administration.

Cybersecurity is part of every employee’s role. A stolen password, a rushed click, an unlocked laptop or an incorrectly shared file can give an attacker an opportunity to access business systems. Good security reduces the likelihood of fraud, data loss, service disruption and harm to customers or colleagues. Early reporting also gives the organisation more time to contain an incident.
Explain confidentiality, integrity and availability in an everyday workplace context.
Recognise common threats such as phishing, malware, weak passwords, unauthorised access and accidental disclosure.
Apply safer behaviours when using accounts, devices, email, websites and business information.
Use the organisation’s approved process to report suspicious activity or a mistake.
Describe how an employee action can affect business operations, privacy, trust and legal obligations.
The CIA triad: confidentiality, integrity and availability
Security as a shared workplace responsibility

Confidentiality means information is seen only by people who need and are allowed to see it. Integrity means information is correct, complete and protected from unauthorised changes. Availability means approved users can access systems and information when they need them. A single event can affect all three: ransomware may prevent access to files, alter or encrypt them, and expose stolen copies.

A threat is a potential source of harm, such as a criminal sending a fake invoice. A vulnerability is a weakness, such as a reused password or an unpatched device. Risk is the chance and impact of the threat succeeding. Employees reduce risk by following procedures, checking unusual requests and reporting weaknesses rather than trying to hide them.

Use your own account and keep credentials private. Do not share passwords or approve a login request that you did not initiate. Access should match a person’s work needs. If you no longer need access, or notice access that seems excessive, contact the appropriate support or security team.

Lock your screen when stepping away. Install updates through approved channels and do not disable security tools without authorisation. Unapproved software, removable media and browser extensions can introduce malware or expose information.

Before sending, storing or discussing information, check who should receive it and whether the method is approved. Use approved storage and sharing tools, verify recipients, and avoid placing sensitive business information in personal accounts or public services.

Report unusual messages, lost devices, unexpected login alerts, suspected malware, accidental disclosure and other concerns promptly using the organisation’s approved reporting channel. Do not delay because you are unsure or worried about blame. Fast reporting improves the chance of containment and recovery.
An employee receives an unexpected request to buy gift cards. They verify the request using a known phone number instead of replying to the email.
A staff member notices a login approval on their phone while they are not signing in. They deny it and report the alert.
A laptop is left unattended in a shared meeting room. The employee locks the screen and stores the device securely before leaving.
A spreadsheet containing customer details is being sent to an external partner. The sender checks the recipient, confirms the approved sharing method and uses the minimum necessary information.
A user clicks a suspicious link and notices unusual browser behaviour. They disconnect only as instructed by the incident process, contact support and provide the message details.
Use unique passwords and approved multi-factor authentication.
Pause and verify unexpected requests, links, attachments and payment changes.
Lock screens and protect devices in public or shared spaces.
Use approved software, storage, email and collaboration tools.
Share information only with the right people and only when needed.
Keep devices and applications updated through approved processes.
Report mistakes and suspicious activity promptly and honestly.

The module assessment uses one of three question banks: Question Bank A, B or C. Each bank contains 10 questions, with a mixture of multiple-choice and workplace scenario questions. Questions cover the CIA triad, threats and vulnerabilities, account protection, device security, information handling, reporting and business impact. The application should record the selected bank, attempt, answers and score. A different bank should be selected for repeated attempts where available.

Cybersecurity is a shared responsibility built from small, repeatable actions. Protect accounts and information, use approved systems, keep devices secure, verify unusual requests and report concerns quickly. These behaviours help preserve confidentiality, integrity and availability while reducing disruption, financial loss and harm to people.

title: Module 8 – Incident Reporting and Cyber Hygiene

blocks.text: Build reliable daily security habits and report suspicious events quickly so the organisation can contain and recover from incidents.

Employees make decisions about incident reporting and cyber hygiene during ordinary work. A short pause, a verified request and timely reporting can prevent a small warning from becoming a business incident. This module connects practical behaviour with the protection of people, information, services and organisational trust.
